sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: scp (Secure Copy Protocol) copies files and directories between hosts over SSH. It uses SSH for authentication and encryption, so no extra setup is needed beyond an existing SSH configuration. General syntax: scp [options] <source> <destination> Remote paths use the format user@host:/path .

sections.heading: Copy a local file to a remote server
Copy a remote file to the local machine
Copy a directory recursively
sections.text: Use -r to copy a full directory tree. scp -r /local/dir user@host:/remote/path/

sections.heading: Use a specific SSH private key
Use a non-standard SSH port
sections.text: scp -P 2222 /local/file.txt user@host:/remote/path/ NOTE: The port flag for scp is uppercase -P , unlike ssh which uses lowercase -p .

sections.heading: Limit bandwidth usage
sections.text: Value is in Kbits/s. scp -l 1024 /local/file.txt user@host:/remote/path/

sections.heading: Copy with verbose output (useful for debugging)
Common options summary
sections.text: Option Description -r Recursive copy (directories) -P <port> Non-standard SSH port -i <key> Private key file -p Preserve file timestamps and permissions -l <kbps> Limit transfer bandwidth -v Verbose mode -C Enable compression -q Quiet mode (suppress progress)

sections.heading: Notes
sections.text: scp relies on the remote scp binary being present on the target host. For large or frequent transfers, consider rsync over SSH: it supports delta transfers and is more efficient for repeated syncs. On RHEL 9 and newer systems, scp may use the SFTP subsystem by default. If transfers fail, check that Subsystem sftp is enabled in sshd_config .
